title: Microvascular Anastomosis, Thrombosis and Free Flap Monitoring

steps.say: Free flaps are sitting at the top of the reconstructive ladder for a reason. They are used when simpler closure, grafts, and local flaps cannot fill the defect or restore function. A free flap brings its own blood supply on named vessels. That independence is powerful, but it is making the anastomosis the single point of failure.
steps.tx: **Free flaps** (tissue moved with its named artery and vein and reconnected under the microscope) sit at the top of the reconstructive ladder. They are chosen when direct closure, skin grafts, and local flaps cannot fill the defect or restore function. A free flap carries its own blood supply, so survival depends entirely on patent microvascular anastomoses sewn at transfer.

vis.alt: Reconstructive ladder rising from direct closure and grafts through local flaps to free tissue transfer at the top.
vis.caption: The reconstructive ladder: free flaps cap the ladder when simpler rungs cannot restore the defect. Credit: StewardMD.

steps.say: Anastomoses are sewn under the operating microscope with very fine nylon. The usual sizes are 9-0 or 10-0, placed as interrupted or continuous stitches. The adventitia is trimmed back and the lumen is irrigated before suturing. A coloured background strip is placed behind the vessels so the needle can be seen clearly.
steps.tx: **Microvascular anastomoses** (hand-sewn joins between donor and recipient vessels under magnification) are performed under the **operating microscope** (a binocular microscope giving stereoscopic magnified vision) using 9-0 or 10-0 **nylon** (a fine nonabsorbable monofilament suture) in interrupted or continuous fashion. Trimmed adventitia, heparinised irrigation, and a background strip keep the field clean and visible.

steps.say: Matching vessels are joined end to end, which is keeping the flow path straight and simple. When one vessel is much larger, an end to side join is accommodating the mismatch instead. The accepted limit is a size difference greater than one and a half to one and up to two to one. Beyond that limit, a vein graft or a different recipient vessel is being selected.
steps.tx: Choose **end-to-end** (direct circular join of two cut vessel ends) when diameters match, preserving straight laminar flow. Choose **end-to-side** (donor end sewn into a window in the recipient wall) for **size discrepancies** (donor to recipient diameter differences) greater than 1.5:1 to 2:1, since it also preserves distal recipient flow. Spatulation widens a small end before suturing.

steps.say: Veins fail more often than arteries, and the numbers are making this clear. Venous thrombosis is occurring more frequently than arterial thrombosis and is accounting for over 60 percent of all microvascular flap failures. Thin walls, low pressure, and kinking are predisposing the outflow. Two veins are being repaired for every one artery wherever possible.
steps.tx: **Venous thrombosis** (clot forming in the flap outflow vein with congestion behind it) occurs more frequently than **arterial thrombosis** (clot in the inflow artery with an empty pale flap) and accounts for over 60% of all microvascular flap failures. Low venous pressure, thin collapsible walls, pedicle kinking, and external compression explain the difference, so experienced surgeons repair two veins for each artery.

rows: Over 60% of failures, low pressure outflow
Two veins per artery, unkinked pedicle

steps.say: Most clots are forming in the first one to three days, so monitoring is being kept hourly through that window. Colour, temperature, turgor, capillary refill, and pinprick bleeding are being checked every hour for 24 to 72 hours. A flap that looked perfect at midnight can be congested by morning. The night checks are never being skipped.
steps.tx: Microvascular **flap thrombosis** (clot occluding the new anastomosis after transfer) occurs predominantly within the first 24 to 72 hours postoperatively, demanding rigorous hourly **flap monitoring** (scheduled bedside checks of colour, warmth, turgor, refill, and pinprick bleeding). Checks continue through the whole window even when the flap looks perfect, since salvage depends on early detection.

vis.alt: Microsurgical lymphovenous anastomosis under magnification, the same fine vessel technique used in free flap transfer.
vis.caption: Microvascular anastomosis under the microscope: hourly monitoring for 24 to 72 hours protects this join. Credit: StewardMD.

steps.say: A pale cold flap with slow refill is signalling arterial failure. The signs are pallor, capillary refill delayed over 3 seconds, loss of tissue turgor, cool skin temperature, and scant or absent pinprick bleeding that is bright red. The flap looks empty and white. Arterial compromise is requiring immediate return to theatre.
steps.tx: Signs of **arterial compromise** (inflow failure starving the flap of oxygenated blood) include **pallor** (white empty appearance), delayed **capillary refill** (blanch pressure test of skin perfusion) over 3 seconds, loss of tissue turgor, cool skin temperature, and bright red scant or absent **pinprick** (needle prick test of dermal bleeding) bleeding. A pale cool flap with slow refill means the artery is down.

steps.say: A blue swollen flap with brisk dark bleeding is signalling venous failure. The signs are cyanosis, rapid capillary refill under 1 second, tense swelling, and brisk dark venous bleeding upon pinprick. The flap looks full and dusky rather than empty. Venous congestion is being relieved urgently before the blood stagnates and clots.
steps.tx: Signs of **venous congestion** (outflow block with blood trapped inside the flap) include **cyanosis** (blue purple discolouration from deoxygenated blood), rapid capillary refill under 1 second, tense swelling, and brisk dark venous bleeding upon **pinprick**. A dusky swollen flap with fast dark refill means the vein is blocked, which is the more common failure pattern.

steps.say: Speed is determining salvage, so the threshold for re-exploration is being kept low. Urgent surgical re-exploration within 4 to 6 hours of detected vascular insufficiency is salvaging over 70 percent of compromised free flaps. The clot is evacuated, the join is revised, and vein grafts are added when needed. Topical papaverine or lidocaine irrigation is countering spasm, with weight-based heparin prophylaxis supporting patency.
steps.tx: Urgent surgical **re-exploration** (reopening the wound to inspect and revise the anastomosis) within 4 to 6 hours of detected vascular insufficiency salvages over 70% of compromised free flaps, while delay sharply lowers success. **Pharmacological adjuncts** (drugs supporting the repair) include topical **papaverine** or **lidocaine** irrigation to counteract vasospasm and weight-based **heparin** prophylaxis against further thrombosis.
